e.etymology: A feminine form of Tristan, the Celtic name of the knight in the legend of Tristan and Isolde, long associated with French triste, sad.
namesakes: Trista Sutter (the first star of The Bachelorette)

e.etymology: From the English surname meaning son of Roger. Roger is a Germanic name joining the words for fame and spear.
namesakes: Rogers Hornsby (Hall of Fame baseball hitter)

assoc.t: Fred Rogers of Mister Rogers' Neighborhood

e.etymology: A spelling of Krista or Christa, a modern short form of Christina, from Latin Christianus, a follower of Christ.
From an English surname that goes back to the Old English name Waltheof, built on weald, power. American use came from the surname, helped along by Ralph Waldo Emerson.

assoc.t: Waldo of the Where's Waldo? picture books

e.note: Expect Where's Waldo? jokes; the striped picture-book character owns the name for most Americans.

e.etymology: An early 20th-century name of the American South, also spelled Mozell and Moselle. Its source is not documented.
From the occupational surname for a hayward, the village officer who looked after hedges and fences and kept cattle out of the crops.
In Italian a man's name, the form of Daniel, from Hebrew for God is my judge. For girls it follows French Danièle, a spelling of Danielle.
A Spanish-language name used mainly in Puerto Rico and Cuba. It is thought to come from Migdal, the Hebrew word for tower behind Magdala and Magdalena.
From the English color word tawny, a pale orange-brown, which goes back to an Old French word for tanned. It is sometimes also a use of the surname Tawney.
namesakes: Tawny Kitaen (actress in 1980s Whitesnake music videos)

e.etymology: A pet form of Dora with the ending -etta. Dora is short for Dorothea and Theodora, Greek names that join the words for gift and God.
From the name of the Oneida, one of the Iroquois nations, whose name for themselves means people of the standing stone. Counties, towns and a lake in New York carry it too.

assoc.t: the Oneida, a Native American nation

e.note: It is the name of a living Native American nation, which some families will want to weigh before using it.

e.etymology: A spelling of Sabrina, the Roman-era name of the River Severn in Britain and of the river's nymph in Milton's masque Comus.
The family nickname of the Roman statesman Marcus Tullius Cicero, from Latin cicer, chickpea. Americans of the 1800s gave it to sons in his honor.

assoc.t: Cicero, the Roman statesman and orator

e.etymology: A respelling of Christian, from Latin Christianus, a follower of Christ.
From a northern English surname for someone who lived by a holm, an islet or patch of dry ground in a river meadow.
From an English occupational surname for the man in charge of a mill. It spread as a first name in honor of President Millard Fillmore.
A spelling of Brittany, the English name of the Breton region of France, from Medieval Latin Britannia. It was a hit American name of the 1980s and 1990s.
A pet form of Laurence, from Latin Laurentius, and of Roland, a Frankish name meaning famous land.
A phonetic spelling of Caitlin, the Irish form of Katherine, which arrived by way of Old French Cateline. English speakers began saying it KAYT-lin in the 1970s, which set off many respellings.
A modern feminine form of Charles, which goes back to a Germanic word for a free man.
A spelling of Stephanie that keeps the look of Stephen. Stephanie came from French Stéphanie, the feminine of Stephen, from Greek stephanos, crown or garland.
namesakes: Stephenie Meyer (author of the Twilight novels)

e.etymology: An older spelling of Katie, the pet form of Katherine.
Tied to Delphi, the site of the ancient Greek oracle, like the French name Delphine. In America it was sometimes also a short form of Philadelphia.
A French pet form of Barbara and of Elisabeth, made with the diminutive ending -ette.
namesakes: Babette (the French cook in the film Babette's Feast)

e.etymology: Built from Lu, as in Lucy or Louise, with the diminutive ending -etta.
A spelling of Jermaine, the English form of French Germain, from Latin Germanus, a name that meant both brother and a German.
A pet form of Hugh, a Norman name from the Germanic word hug, mind or spirit.
namesakes: Hughie Campbell (protagonist of the series The Boys)

e.etymology: From an Old High German name joining waltan, to rule, and mari, famous. It merged with Scandinavian Valdemar, the form of Vladimir borne by Danish kings, and reached English in the 19th century.
The medieval English form of Margaret, taken from Old French and ultimately from Greek margarites, pearl. Marjorie is the same name in another spelling.
namesakes: Margery Williams (author of The Velveteen Rabbit)

e.etymology: The short form of Rodney and Roderick. Roderick starts with the Germanic word for fame; Rodney is an English place-name surname.
namesakes: Rod Serling (creator of The Twilight Zone)
e.note: Rod is also an ordinary word for a pole or bar and has some crude slang uses.

e.etymology: A pet form of Gertrude, a Germanic name joining ger, spear, and a word for strength.
